A hand-drawn, xkcd-style line graph titled “Over time, I got better at telling the difference.” The y-axis is labeled “Probability” and runs from 0.0 to 1.0. The x-axis is labeled “Time” and runs from 1/1/2025 to “Today,” with ticks every two months (1/1/2025, 3/1/2025, 5/1/2025, 7/1/2025, 9/1/2025, 11/1/2025).

Two lines are plotted. A red line, labeled “Probability that Claude just said something ridiculous,” starts at about 0.92 in January 2025 and declines steadily to about 0.5 by November 2025. A blue line, labeled “Probability that I just misunderstood what Claude said,” starts at about 0.07 in January 2025 and rises steadily to about 0.5 by November 2025.

The two lines meet at 0.5 at a vertical dashed line marked “Opus 4.5 (Nov 2025).” After that point the trends speed up: the red line drops sharply to about 0.24 by “Today,” and the blue line climbs sharply to about 0.78. The joke is that the author’s growing skill at “telling the difference” mostly consists of realizing that, with newer Claude models, the confusing part is increasingly their own misunderstanding rather than Claude’s mistake.

LLM red teaming has the following defining characteristics: 

    It’s limit-seeking: Red teamers find boundaries and explore limits in system behavior.
    It’s never malicious: People doing red teaming are not interested in doing harm—in fact, quite the opposite.
    It’s manual: Being a creative and playful practice, the parts of red teaming that can be automated are often most useful to give human red teamers insight for their work.
    It’s a team effort: Practitioners find inspiration in each others’ techniques and prompts, and the norm is to respect fellow practitioners’ work.
    It’s approached with an alchemist mindset: We found that red teamers tend to abandon rationalizations about models and their behavior and instead embrace the chaotic and unknown nature of the work.

· Thought · 6.8s

P17 finding documented: FastCGI SetHandler canonical SCRIPT_FILENAME RCE.

At HEAD b0f6b8d5, fastcgi::handler target for file still builds the wire SCRIPT_FILENAME from actual_path (the canonical symlink target), even though Target.script_filename is documented as the lexical request-mapped value and P15 fixed the ProxyPassMatch/PATH_INFO constructor. PHP-FPM therefore applies security.limit_extensions to a different name than Apache.

Observed chain - global/per-directory SetHandler, uploads hardened with SetHandler none, and an in-root symlink:

/uploads/shell.php          -> static source on both servers
/pub/upload-link.txt -> ../uploads/shell.php

· Apache: 403 Access denied. - FPM sees pub/upload-link.txt (.txt)
· vapahe: 200 PHPEXEC uploads-shell uid=33 - FPM sees uploads/shell.php (.php)

The FPM access log confirms the drift (Apache lexical vs vapahe canonical). Case C demonstrates the same result through an access-file proxy handler; case D shows canonical <Location>/<Directory> denials still bind, so this is a backend policy-gate bypass, not an auth-guard bypass.

Files added/updated

· adversarial/findings_p17.md - root cause, exploit chain, evidence, impact, fix, scope.
· adversarial/p17/exploit_p17.py - 15-verdict differential harness (cases A-D), rerun successfully: 15 verdict(s) passed.
· adversarial/README.md - P17 index entry and reproduction section.

No product source was modified. The benchmark ProxyPassMatch branch remains fixed by P15; P17 affects the documented SetHandler deployment class when the handler scope covers the lexical non-PHP name (global/per-directory or access-file handler).
